variations.basis: Varied for this scenario (was 2.1): the high end of the range given for a year's extension, [0.61, 3.05] m. No measurement of a season's extension of wisteria was found in any paper, flora, RHS record or in Bean; the US Forest Service's review says "Rates and distances of spread are not known". The range is the one published statement that gives both ends, Ohio State University's plant record for the genus: "stems during the current season's growth are virtually unbranched, often growing from two to ten feet during the growing season", and "up to ten feet per year under optimum conditions"; in metres. It is said of any stem of the season, in the heat of an American summer, so its low end is low for a leading stem and its high end is a ceiling for a British one. The value is the one figure found for a British garden, at second hand from a nursery's blog: "around seven feet of new growth in one season" (https://blog.thompson-morgan.com/wisteria-masterclass-best-expert-content). Until 14 November 2026 the prototype's 2.6 m stood here. Not measured: the first number to measure on a plant.

Varied for this scenario (was [0.5,0.8]): the high end of the range given for the first seasons after planting. What is published is how long the slow start lasts, not how slow it is: "often slow to establish during its first one to two years of growth, but grows very rapidly thereafter" (Ohio State University, of the genus); "Can be slow to establish" (Missouri Botanical Garden, of this species). The range is that span of time: two slow seasons at its low end, one at its high end, and the value lies between them. The half that a slow season is taken to make is the Wisteria prototype's and has no published counterpart. A trial in Tokyo had large pot-grown Wisteria floribunda reach the end of a 2 m trellis within four months of planting (https://www.tokyo-aff.or.jp/uploaded/attachment/6274.pdf), so a big nursery plant, watered, need not be slow at all.

Varied for this scenario (was 0.7): the high end of the range given for a year's extension, [0.3, 0.8] m. RHS guide: "It is relatively slow growing, but in favourable conditions can eventually reach 4m (14ft) or more" (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/trachelospermum/growing-guide). Bean has it 10 or 12 ft high on walls in the south and west, and "rather slow-growing when young". The range: at the low end a British nursery's "2 - 3m over 10 years" (https://www.architecturalplants.com/product/trachelospermum-jasminoides-int1cav1/, which also says "Approximately 50cm annually"); at the high end the slow end of the RHS record's band, 8 m in ten years. The faster end of that band, 2.4 m a year, is not what the RHS's own guide or British growers describe, and "rapid" is said of it only in the south-eastern United States. 0.7 m takes a main stem to the top of a 3 m support in its fifth or sixth season. Not measured.

notes: Hours are direct sun on a clear day in the middle of the month, as the geometry allows: not sunshine records. A half-shaded minute counts as half.
Shares compare a place with an open site at the same spot, so cloud, which falls on both alike, is not in them.
Shade comes from the timber and cables, from what the site declares, and from the leaf other plants carried the season before. A plant is not counted as shading itself.
Warmth, shelter and wind are not light and are not modelled: where a profile asks for a warm or sheltered aspect, nothing here speaks to that.
